candidates.text:
The Arsenal Fit: Ezri Konsa

Hello all. Thank you for once again tuning into another one of my detailed reports. This time on our newest addition Ezri Konsa! In today's report I'll discuss his profile and his fit as an #AFC player. Feel free to drop your thoughts in the comments below. All feedback is welcomed.

My short form A4 report is attached as an image too.

Ezri Konsa is the type of signing I would personally describe as a floor raiser. He is not necessarily arriving to completely transform our backline, but as depth he raises the level considerably.

Konsa can play at both CB and RB, has 7 full seasons of Premier League experience and has represented his country on numerous occasions, making 8 apps at the World Cup (28 caps). At around 6”0 and 77kg, his lean build does not make him the most physically imposing CB, but he combines excellent recovery pace, spatial awareness, agility, 1v1 defending and his most outstanding quality; calmness. He rarely looks rushed, rarely overcommits and generally tends to make the right decisions.

The reliability that he offers is crucial in the current predicament we are in. With Saliba unavailable for the foreseeable, we need someone capable of stepping into the backline without shifting the excellent balance that Arteta has built. Konsa obviously does not replicate everything Saliba provides, but he gives us ability in a high line, versatility and strong availability.

The Key USP: Defensive Security, Calmness and Reliability

Konsa’s defensive data is slightly unusual as his overall volume is extremely low. He averaged only 5.81 defensive contributions per 90 last season (1st percentile). He averaged 0.65 tackles per 90 (7th percentile) and 0.68 interceptions per 90 (13th percentile). However, I believe those numbers require a lot of context because of how Villa defend under Emery.

Under Emery, Villa attempt to compress the pitch using a highline mid-block, deploying the offside trap selectively rather than continuously, like they have done in previous seasons (record 167 offsides in 23/24). This high positioning, combined with a relentless man-to-man press, allowed Villa to prioritise midfield turnovers and stop opposition attacks before their backline were even forced to intervene. This naturally suppresses defensive contribution numbers. What interests me much more is how efficient he is when he actually has to engage. Konsa won 73% of his ground duels despite only winning 2.0 per 90, ranking him as the highest ground duel winner amongst all Premier League CBs. Further, he was also dribbled past only 0.12 times per 90 (90th percentile – 4 times across the season) and committed just 0.33 fouls per 90 (88th percentile).

IMO, that explains the context of his numbers quite well. Konsa is cautious rather than passive. He does not constantly jump out of the backline looking to win the ball immediately like Romero (he was an alternative option a few weeks ago). Konsa is more comfortable delaying the attacker, controlling the space and choosing the correct moment to engage. I personally see that temperament as a clear similarity to William Saliba. Not necessarily in level, but in the way that both are comfortable allowing the more aggressive CB alongside them to attack the first duel (Pau Torres performed more man to man actions than Konsa last szn).

That is why I think the fit alongside Gabriel makes so much sense. Gabriel naturally wants to step forward, engage early and defend aggressively on the front foot. Konsa gives him the security to continue to do that because he is comfortable operating as the covering CB. His 0.86 blocks per 90 (59th percentile) also support what the eye test suggests; he reads shots well, is composed as a last man defender and rarely panics when the opposition reaches the box.

Physical Profile and Recovery Defending

Konsa’s physical profile should translate extremely well as there are some clear similarities between the defensive environments at Villa and Arsenal. Both teams are comfortable holding a high line and asking the CBs to defend large spaces behind them. Emery has employed a vigorous offside trap in previous seasons, suggesting that Konsa has experience in judging when to step, when to hold off and when to turn and recover at pace.

IMO, his recovery ability is his standout physical trait. Konsa recorded a top speed of around 33.3 kmph last season, which is incredibly quick for a CB and even higher than Christian Mosquera’s recorded 32.9 kmph. He also has excellent hip mobility and can turn quickly when the ball is played in behind the defensive line. Another useful trait is his ability to defend on his weaker side.

I think this gives us something we occasionally lack. Elite recovery pace. Our structure is obviously designed to stop transitions before they develop, but there will always be moments where the press is broken or a ball is played over the top. Konsa gives us another CB, alongside Mosquera, who can recover against quick attackers rather than immediately forcing the entire defensive line to retreat 5-10 yards.

I must note that there are some physical limitations. At 6”0 and 77kg, he is not the most dominant aerial CB. He won only 0.95 aerial duels per 90 at a 57.1% success rate (43rd percentile), which is respectable rather than exceptional.
Comparing him to our current CBS:
- Gabriel: 3.24 aerial duels won per 90 at 62.3%
- Saliba: 2.51 aerial duels won per 90 at 55.3%
- Mosquera: 1.82 aerial duels won per 90 at 41.7%
The data proves he is far less aerially engaged than our current CBs. While his role will demand more aerial output this season, this could become a vulnerability in matches where we have to defend repeated crosses or direct long balls...

However, interestingly, the same limitation does not completely translate to attacking set pieces. Both of his goals last season (UEL) came from corners. Konsa has an incredible vertical leap, strong jump timing and strong box movement when he attacks crosses.

Passing Profile

This is probably the biggest tactical question surrounding the 28 year old.

He is an exceptionally safe passer. He completed 59.38 passes per 90 last season at an incredible 95.5% accuracy, the highest success rate amongst Prem CBs (100th percentile). His long ball volume was relatively low at 1.81 per 90 (34th percentile), but he completed an unbelievable 61% of those attempts (98th percentile), again showing how strong his retention is.

It is important to mention that his passing style is much more about retention and security than progression. Konsa is excellent at shifting the ball laterally and backwards, returning possession to his CB partner and waiting for the opposition press to move before playing again. There is real value in that. Repeated safe circulation can drag pressing structures from side to side, force opp forwards to keep working and eventually create space elsewhere. Further, his 1.19 fouls won per 90 (89th percentile), also reflects how secure he is when opponents press him.

However, there is a clear difference between retention and progression. Konsa ranked only in the:
- 35th percentile for progressive passes
- 54th percentile for passes into the final third
- 38th percentile for xThreat generated through live passes
- 82nd percentile for forward passes, but a lot of those actions are safer passes to wide areas rather than vertical progression

Comparing him to Saliba in these metrics is important to illustrate the differences:
- 79th percentile for progressive passes
- 82nd for passes into the final third
- 78th for xThreat from live passing

Thus, with Konsa directly replacing Saliba for the foreseeable future, we will clearly lose some progression from the back. That does not make Konsa a poor fit, but it does mean that the responsibility of backline progression has to be redistributed elsewhere – more on that later…

Dribbling and Carrying Profile:

Konsa is slightly more comfortable progressing through carrying than his passing numbers might suggest, although I would personally not describe him as a high volume carrier. He ranked:
- 46th percentile for progressive carries
- 43rd percentile for xThreat via progressive carries
- 31st percentile for carries into the final third.

His carrying profile is quite simple to describe. If the opposition leaves space in front of him, he will move into it, invite the presser and then release possession once that player jumps. He is not someone who constantly drives through midfield or tries to get past multiple players in one move.

This follows the theme of my profile description quite well. Konsa is fundamentally a safe circulation option who is comfortable moving into space available to him without forcing the next action. I would expect that to remain unchanged within our system.

Injury/Availability Note:

Konsa’s injury history is another massive positive. Across his Villa career, he has missed only 11 matches through injury, with his last recorded injury absence coming in February 2025.

Last season he featured an incredible 48 times for Villa and another 8 times for England at the World Cup, accumulating around 4,817 minutes. For comparison, Gabriel recorded around 4,660 minutes across Arsenal and Brazil.

The durability he offers is extremely valuable, particularly with Saliba unavailable and our RB options being quite injury prone. Konsa gives us another defender who has shown he can handle a significant workload without needing to be carefully managed throughout the season.

The Arsenal Fit: Ezri Konsa

My preferred use of Konsa would be at RCB alongside Gabriel. The defensive relationship is the main reason I like the fit.

Gabriel naturally tends to defend further forward, engage CFs early and attack the first duel. Konsa, like Saliba, is more cautious and controlled in engagement. He is comfortable delaying the attacker, protecting the space behind the action and waiting for the correct moment to commit.

It is not exactly the Gabriel x Saliba partnership, but the temperament is similar. Gabriel can continue being the aggressive defender while Konsa provides the calmer presence alongside him.

Konsa’s recovery pace also helps that relationship. If Gabriel steps out and the first defensive action is beaten, Konsa has the speed and awareness to recover towards goal or cover across. That should allow us to continue to defend high without Gabriel having to change the way he operates.

The bigger concern for me comes in possession. At RCB, Konsa can circulate safely towards the right side, find the midfielder ahead of him or recycle possession back across the defensive line. However, if he remains as conservative as he was at Villa, we will lose some of the progression that Saliba normally provides.

That would make Gabriel the obvious progressive outlet from the back. This could lead to an issue as against stronger pressing teams, his circulation may be too predictable. Opponents would allow Konsa to circulate safely before jumping aggressively when the ball finds Gabriel, effectively making him a pressing trigger. We would then need another route through the first line, whether that comes from Rice or MLS dropping deeper, or from Konsa simply being encouraged to take slightly more risk.

Refer to Image 1

I also think that Konsa would work well as the CCB in our 3-2-5.

His extremely safe sideways and backwards passing suits a central circulation role. He can receive, move the opposition press from side to side and recycle through either CB without losing possession. In that sense, he could definitely help us remain patient and gradually exhaust the opposition's press.

The limitation is similar though. If the CCB offers very little vertical progression, opponents may eventually stop jumping towards him and instead focus on closing the players around him. That could again place more pressure on Gabriel or the midfielders dropping into the backline.

Refer to Image 2

So whether he plays RCB or CCB, the trade-off is relatively simple to explain. Konsa gives us exceptional security and calmness on and off the ball, but the structure around him may need to compensate for some of the progression we lose from the absence of Saliba

Brief Tactical Note: Konsa as a RB

Konsa’s ability to cover RB adds another useful layer to his profile, especially due to the injury prone nature of both Timber and White.

Unlike Timber’s inverted role, he will likely play more conservatively within the 3-2-5. If he starts games at RB I’d expect him to offer flank support and serve as a safe circulation option, mimicking Ben White's approach. His primary task would be locking down a tricky LW, a role where his strong 1v1 defensive traits will shine.

There is also a potentially interesting butterfly effect for our build-up play. If Konsa is naturally more conservative on the right (especially with forward movements), we may be encouraged to progress more frequently through the LHS rather than constantly building through our usual right sided combinations with Ode and Saka.

I would treat that as more of a possibility than something guaranteed, but his profile certainly gives Arteta the option to structure the team that way.

Final Verdict

Like I said in the intro, I see Ezri Konsa as a very strong floor raising signing for our defensive depth.

His defensive reliability, composure, recovery pace and experience in a high line should translate naturally, while his ability to play at both CB and RB raises the quality of our depth considerably. His availability also makes him a valuable asset as we could play 60+ games again this season.

However, there are limitations. His progressive passing is clearly weaker than Saliba’s and his aerial profile is only average for a CB. We may therefore see Gabriel or the midfield structure around Konsa taking on more responsibility in progression.

For me, the Gabriel partnership is the part that makes the most sense. Konsa’s cautious temperament should allow Gabriel to continue defending aggressively rather than forcing us to completely alter the balance of the back line while Saliba is unavailable.

More broadly, I think the signing reflects Arsenal’s shift towards adding proven players who can immediately solidify the squad. Konsa may not completely transform the ceiling of the team, but he gives us a highly reliable, Premier League proven defender who can step into multiple roles without substantially lowering the level. 

That is exactly why I would describe him as a floor raiser.

Thank you all for reading. I really hope you enjoyed the report! I’d be interested to hear where you see Konsa fitting best. As a RCB, CCB or even as a defensive RB option? 

As always, any feedback or disagreements are welcome. Thank you!

Now, let's talk about him (informal scouting report), a player I have been hyping for days and who, I believe provides us the perfect balance of instant impact and upside potential.

According to what I have seen, he profiles as an explosive, direct attacker with elite one-versus-one dribbling ability and a strong goalscoring threat from wide areas. His game is built around carrying the ball into dangerous positions, cutting inside onto his stronger left foot, and either shooting or creating chances for teammates. Does that sound familiar to my fellow City fans?

Playing Style and Tactical Role:

- Functions best as a right-sided inside forward in possession-based systems that allow him freedom to drift infield and attack spaces between the lines.

- When receiving the ball in the final third, his first instincts are typically to drive forward with dribbles or look for shooting opportunities.

- One thing to note is that his progressive carrying is exceptional, ranking in the 93rd percentile among comparable wingers, which makes him an effective ball-progressor from wide areas.

- While primarily a goal threat, he also ranks above average for progressive passes and dangerous passes, indicating he can link play and provide for teammates, though this remains a secondary skill compared to his dribbling and shooting.

Let's discuss his strengths:

1. 1v1 Dribbling:
- Possesses elite ball control and the ability to beat defenders in tight spaces. 
- His unpredictable changes of pace and direction make him extremely difficult to mark in isolation. 
- Ranks in the 84th percentile for successful take-ons and consistently completes dribbles at a high rate.

2. Progressive Ball Carrying:
- His capacity to drive forward with the ball and break defensive lines is among his standout attributes. 
- Ranking in the 93rd percentile for progressive carries, he consistently advances play from wide areas into the final third.

3. Final Third Threat:
- Ranks in the 96th percentile for touches in the attacking penalty area and the 89th percentile for non-penalty goals per 90 minutes.

4. Set-Piece Delivery:
- Offers additional creative value through accurate corner and free-kick delivery, adding another dimension to his attacking contribution.

5. Chance Creation:
- He ranks in the 96th percentile for chances created, highlighting his ability to generate scoring opportunities for teammates in addition to his own goal threat.

Now, the weaknesses.

1. Defensive Work Rate:
- His defensive contributions rank in the 7th percentile, indicating limited involvement in tracking back, pressing, and defensive positioning.  
- His defensive numbers are generally below average, though his defensive duel success rate remains solid.  This is an area with significant room for improvement and Maresca would have to work a lot with him on that aspect.

2. Aerial Duels:
- He ranks in the 34th percentile for aerial duels won, limiting his effectiveness both offensively and defensively in aerial situations.

3. Pass Completion and Build-up Involvement:
- His pass completion rate ranks in the 21st percentile at approximately 67.9 percent, reflecting inconsistency in build-up play.  
- This is partly a symptom of his direct attacking style, which prioritizes forward carries and shots over safe circulation, but it can limit his effectiveness in systems requiring high possession retention. An area of massive improvement.

4. Tactical Discipline
- Still developing his off-ball movement and understanding of defensive shape. 
- His positioning when not in possession can be inconsistent, and he occasionally loses track of overlapping fullbacks. Elite coaching can help improve this aspect.

My honest opinion (executive summary): 
Moussa is a high-upside, left-footed right winger (which is what we need) with elite one-versus-one dribbling, exceptional progressive carrying, and a proven goalscoring threat from wide areas.

He is ideally suited to possession-based systems that value direct attacking play (vertical patterns) and can benefit from his ability to break down low-block defenses (should I talk further about low-blocks to a City fan, eh?)

I believe that his primary areas for development lie in defensive work rate, pass completion in build-up phases, and tactical discipline when out of possession, however, he would be an amazing addition to our squad.

One decision changed three franchises forever.

Here are 5 Things You Need To Know After Week 2 Of The NFL Preseason 🏈 

1. Jadarian Price’s Stock Is Rising 📈

The Seahawks have bubble-wrapped Price in the preseason and have stated that he’s not going to play in any of the games. It’s increasingly looking like he’ll be the Seahawks’ RB1 in Week 1, with George Holani handling the passing down snaps. He should be an easy click at his current ADP.

2. Tony Pollard’s Stock Is Falling 📉📉

Through two preseason games, Pollard has played only 41% of offensive snaps with Cam Ward as the starter. Meanwhile, Tyjae Spears has seen 59% of the snaps with Cam. It’s increasingly looking like the Titans will use a running back by committee approach this season.

I’m out on Tony Pollard in fantasy.

3. Matthew Golden Is in for a Breakout Season ⭐️

Golden had a beautiful rep in the Packers’ game against the Broncos, beating PS2 for a 19-yard gain. He also hauled in another tough catch over the middle of the field against Justin Strnad (on a play where he was interfered with). 

Golden was one of my favorite route runners coming out of the 2025 draft, and it looks like he’s headed for a massive 2026 season. One of the reasons why the Packers let Wicks and Doubs walk in free agency is because of Matthew Golden’s presence.

Buy the hype 📈

4. Camden Brown Should Make the Cowboys’ 53-Man Roster ⭐️

Through the first two preseason games, Camden Brown has piled up 135 receiving yards and 2 touchdowns. He’s been a solid option against man coverage and looks like a massive steal for the Cowboys.

The Cowboys have done a good job over the past couple of seasons finding gems at the WR position. Turpin and Flournoy, for example.

In his final season at Georgia Southern, Brown averaged 2.52 YPRR against man coverage. Just turn on the film and watch this guy play, he’s absolutely electric. He should easily make the team over Mingo, IMO.

5. The De’Zhaun Stribling Hype Is Real 📈

Through the first two preseason games, Stribling has accumulated 13 targets. He easily looks like the Niners’ second-best wide receiver on the roster and looks like a star in the making. After the media clowned this draft pick a couple of months ago, the Niners ultimately made the right call on Stribling.

He’s going to make a real impact this season.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
